Transient

A transient analysis solves the circuit in time, from a starting state, with every source playing its waveform. It answers what happens on the way to a steady state, or when there is none: a pulse's edge, a converter's start-up, a reflection. This page covers when to use it instead of harmonic balance or the envelope, setting it up, reading its results, running it on ngspice, and starting harmonic balance from it.

When to use it, and when not

circuitRF is a harmonic-balance simulator first. Transient sits beside it for the questions harmonic balance and the envelope do not answer:

  • Edges and pulses: rise time, overshoot, ringing and settling of a filter or an amplifier driven by a step or a pulse train.
  • Reflections: a pulse travelling a line and coming back from a mismatch.
  • Start-up and settling: a supply, a bias network or a switching converter from power-on.
  • Circuits with no periodic steady state, or whose steady state is the thing in question: a converter's ripple, a relaxation oscillator.
  • A start for harmonic balance on circuits it struggles to start from DC: see Starting harmonic balance from a transient run.

It is the wrong tool for a steady-state RF question. A 1 GHz amplifier's output power, gain, efficiency and harmonics are a harmonic-balance run of a fraction of a second; a transient run has to step through every carrier period until the bias network settles, which can be millions of them. A modulated signal (ACLR, EVM, AM-AM) is the envelope's question: it follows the modulation without resolving the carrier. circuitRF says so when a bench asks transient for that kind of answer (below).

The analysis

Add a Transient analysis to a test bench from Simulate ▸ Setup Analyses. In a netlist it is one line:

analysis TR1 type=tran Stop=10n Step=5p
analysis TR2 type=tran Stop=200u Step=10n InitialState=zero Method=gear2 Solver=ngspice

The card shows Stop, Step, Method, InitialState and Solver; the rest are under More. Every value can be an expression.

Key Default
Stop required End time (s)
Step Stop/1000 The output grid's spacing (s), and the largest step unless MaxStep says otherwise
Start 0 The first reported time; the run still starts at 0
MaxStep auto The largest step: the smaller of Step and 1/(20 f) for the highest frequency any source carries
Method trap trap (trapezoidal: second order, no numerical damping) or gear2 (second-order backward difference: damps ringing). Either takes two backward-Euler steps at the start and after every corner of a source
RelTol, VTol, ITol 1e-3, 1e-6 V, 1e-12 A Tolerances on each Newton update and each step's error estimate
InitialState op op: start from the DC operating point. zero: start from zero, with no DC solve (below)
IC Net voltages held during the operating-point solve: IC="out=5.5, bias=1.2"
Solver native native, circuitRF's own engine, or ngspice (below)
SaveSteps no yes adds the engine's own accepted steps (Steps.time, Steps.V) beside the output grid
MaxSteps 10,000,000 The run is refused before it starts when Stop/MaxStep exceeds it
SpiceOptions, SpiceLines, SpiceLineFreq, SpiceFit ngspice only (below), enabled on the card only with that solver

trap is the default because it does not damp: a lossless resonator rings for as long as it should. If a run shows a small oscillation that flips sign every step after an abrupt edge, that is trapezoidal ringing, and gear2 removes it.

Sources and the switch

The waveform sources exist for transient, one type per waveform, each with a voltage (V_) and a current (I_) form: V_Pulse (a pulse train, or a step when Width is blank), V_PWL (piecewise linear, from points or a file), V_Exp, V_SFFM (a frequency-modulated sine) and V_Expr (any expression in time). In every other analysis each is a constant, its value at t = 0. Idc is the DC current source.

Every corner of a waveform (a pulse's edges, a PWL vertex) is a time the engine lands a step on exactly, so an edge is never smeared across a step.

The tone sources run in transient as sines: V_1Tone, I_1Tone, P1Tone and PnTone, with three keys only a transient reads: Delay (the tone starts then), Ramp (it rises over this time along a raised cosine) and Damping (it decays after Delay). A P1Tone keeps its available power and source impedance, and its harmonic terminations Z[k] are presented at their harmonics.

The voltage-controlled switch, VSwitch, is a resistance between Ron and Roff set by a control voltage, with a smooth transition between Voff and Von, so it works in every analysis. Transient adds Hyst (hysteresis) and TransitionPoints: the step is held short while the control crosses, at least eight steps per crossing by default.

The starting state and initial conditions

With InitialState=op (the default) the run starts from the DC operating point, with every source at its t = 0 value. With InitialState=zero every voltage and current starts at zero and nothing is solved first: the supplies switch on at t = 0, which is how a start-up from power-on is simulated.

Initial conditions set the stored energy the run starts with:

  • On the analysis, IC="out=5.518" holds net out at 5.518 V while the operating point is solved, and releases it at t = 0.
  • On a part, a capacitor's IC is its starting voltage and an inductor's IC its starting current.

Both apply under either InitialState. Their use is to skip a start-up when only the steady state is wanted: the Buck Converter example reads the output voltage and the inductor current at the start of a switching cycle from a run from rest, and starts a second bench there, steady from its first cycle, in 10 µs instead of 200 µs. Setting one of the two alone does not work: the energy left out rings through the filter again.

The output grid and the step

The engine takes steps of its own size, short where the circuit moves fast, long where it does not, and reports every waveform on a uniform grid from Start to Stop at Step, interpolated within each accepted step at the integration's own order. The grid sets what you see; the tolerances set how accurate it is. MaxStep caps the step, and by default follows the fastest source, so a 1 GHz tone gets at least 20 steps a period. SaveSteps=yes keeps the engine's own steps as well, to see where it worked hardest.

The result carries the run's counters, Tran.AcceptedSteps, Tran.RejectedSteps, Tran.NewtonIterations and Tran.Factorizations: a run with many rejected steps is a circuit that is hard to step, not a slow computer.

What runs in time

Elements In a transient run
Resistors, capacitors, inductors, mutual inductance, the transformer, controlled sources, ports and terms Exact
Diodes, BJTs, the FET laws, MOS models, SDDs, Verilog-A devices, nonlinear capacitors, composed FETs As they are: every device evaluates exactly as in harmonic balance
A lossless line, a lossless coupled pair Exact, as delays. The run's message gives the delay and the error against the line's model
A lossy microstrip, stripline, coplanar or ideal line Its delay and a rational fit of the rest, checked against the model up to the run's highest frequency, 1/(2 MaxStep). A line that cannot be fitted within 1e-3 of |S21| there is refused by name with its error
SnP blocks, filters, Z(freq) blocks, tapers, EM cells A rational fit from DC to the run's highest frequency, made passive if it is not, its error and any correction reported. Data that stops short of DC is extrapolated and the run says so
MOD_Source Its signal on its carrier, over a window of its record (Modulated sources)
Lossy coupled lines, mixers and system amplifiers, the Phased Antenna Array, the Propagation Channel, tuners, the WSProbe, the EM Field Data block Refused by name, each with the analysis that does run it

A term or port is a load of its Z in transient, as in harmonic balance.

Results, measurements and the Transient preset

Every labelled net's voltage and every IProbe's current are recorded with nothing to set: V[time, node], I[time, branch], the instantaneous power P through each IProbe, Vprobe (the voltage at its first net) and OP.V, the starting state.

The time-domain functions read them in measure lines: rise, fall, overshoot, undershoot, settle, period, frequency, value_at, tmin, tmax, avg, rms, fft, fft_power and thd. fft of the last period is shaped like a harmonic-balance spectrum, so a trace written for one plots the other.

When a run ends, the Messages panel offers Open Transient plots, and a Data Display's Add Transient button (the sine-wave icon) does the same for its source: the recorded voltages against time, the output's spectrum over its last period (the power through the IProbe whose name says "out", or the output net's voltage), and the bench's measures as a table. Every trace is an ordinary trace to re-point afterwards.

Modulated sources

A MOD_Source plays its signal in a native transient run, carrier-resolved: its LTE, NR, QAM, FSK, chirp or imported I/Q record on its carrier Fc, behind its Z. Use it where the envelope analysis assumes too much: a switching or saturating stage driven by a real modulated signal, a modulated signal beside an unrelated tone, a start-up while the modulation runs, or a check of an envelope result on the same bench. Otherwise the envelope analysis answers a modulated question in a fraction of the time.

A run plays a window of the record, since every carrier cycle is stepped: 10 µs of a 2.4 GHz carrier is about half a million steps, a whole 1 ms record fifty times that. Two keys on the source pick the window:

Key on the MOD_Source Default
RecordStart 0 Where in the record the run starts (s). The record repeats, so any time is a place in it
Ramp 0 A raised-cosine rise of the drive over this time (s), so the circuit is not hit with the signal at full power

Every other analysis ignores both. ngspice does not play a MOD_Source.

What the run keeps is the tran card's Store:

Key on the tran directive Default
Store auto baseband: the envelopes about Fc, at the signal's own sample rate. rf: every output point of the waveform. auto is baseband when the bench has a MOD_Source
StoreHarm 3 Baseband: the harmonics of Fc kept, 0 to this
MeasureFrom auto Baseband: where the measurements start (s); auto is after the largest Ramp

Baseband results are the envelope analysis's own: V[time, node, harmonic], I[time, branch, harmonic] and, at every IProbe, the power, the spectrum (PSD), ACLR, EVM, the constellation, AM-AM and the gain, measured by the same code. A plot or measure line written for an envelope run reads a modulated transient unchanged. The run downconverts as it steps and never holds the waveform, so memory stays small however long the window. EVM needs whole symbols: an OFDM symbol is about 70 µs, so a window shorter than that reports no EVM, and says so.

RF keeps the waveform itself, at an output step of 1/20 of the carrier's period unless Step says otherwise, and the card warns how many points that is. Read it with the time-domain functions, as any transient result.

All sources in a baseband run share one Fc and one RecordStart; a bench whose sources differ is refused and names Store=rf.

When circuitRF suggests another analysis

circuitrf explain --analysis on a transient bench reports, without running it, the solver, the step bound and why, roughly how many steps the run will take, and the slowest time constant against Stop:

TR1              tran               TR1                          DISPATCHED by tran
  Solver native
  Step bound 5E-12 s (the output Step): about 1.2E+04 steps over Stop = 6E-08 s at that bound
  Slowest time constant 9.63E-10 s (the network at node 'g'): Stop is 62.3 of them

When Stop spans more than 105 periods of the highest carrier a source plays, it adds a steering line:

  Consider another analysis: this bench is 1·10⁶ periods of a 1 GHz carrier: harmonic balance answers a
  steady-state question in a fraction of the time.

It names the envelope instead when the source is modulated. It is advice, not a refusal: the run still goes, but a bench that simulates a million carrier periods to read one steady state is asking transient a harmonic-balance question. A slowest time constant far longer than Stop means the result has not settled.

ngspice

ngspice is an open-source SPICE simulator circuitRF can run as a second transient solver. circuitRF writes the bench as a SPICE deck, runs ngspice on it as a separate program, and reads its waveforms back into an ordinary result: the same cubes, the same measures, the same plots. It is useful as a check on the native engine, and for a circuit someone already trusts in ngspice.

The set of benches ngspice can run is smaller than the set the native engine runs, on purpose. Every element is translated exactly or refused by name, never approximated without being asked. A bench that uses a microstrip line, an S-parameter block or a FET law runs natively but not on ngspice unless one of the two approximations below is asked for.

Installing. Settings ▸ Solvers lists ngspice under Circuit, below the EM solvers. Install ngspice… fetches upstream's own build, or run circuitrf solver install ngspice. An ngspice from a package manager, on PATH or named by CIRCUITRF_NGSPICE is found with nothing to set. On Windows the program is ngspice's console build, ngspice_con.exe. Details per platform are on the Settings page.

Choosing it. On the transient card, Solver ▸ ngspice. The choice is enabled only while ngspice is found, labelled with its version; a bench that already says ngspice, opened where there is none, shows the choice greyed with a note. Its run is refused with the way to install one. It never falls back to the native engine.

What translates exactly. Resistors, capacitors and inductors (with IC), mutual inductance, the transformer, controlled sources, IProbes, ports and terms, every DC, waveform and tone source, V_Expr/I_Expr, lossless lines, the VSwitch, SDDs, a placed SPICE subcircuit (its file included as it is), Verilog-A devices (ngspice loads the same compiled .osdi), and the diode, BJT and MOS level 1 and 3 models where every parameter maps one to one. Discontinuities whose model is a fixed lumped network (a gap, a bend, an arm-less tee or cross) translate too.

What is refused, and why. A device parameter with no counterpart in ngspice's model of the same name, a device away from its nominal temperature (the two temperature models differ), a MOS with Tox (its gate charge model differs), a pulse with a zero rise, fall or width (ngspice reads zero as its own default), a P1Tone with harmonic terminations Z[k]. Lossy lines, S-parameter blocks, filters, EM cells and frequency-dependent discontinuities have no exact counterpart. The FET laws and composed FETs, system blocks, tuners and probes other than the IProbe have none either. Every refused element is listed at once, with its reason; nothing is run. circuitrf check lists the same refusals before a run.

SpiceLines=rlgc. ngspice has lossy lines described by per-unit-length R, L, G and C (TXL, and CPL for a coupled pair) but none described by geometry and substrate. With SpiceLines=rlgc, each line is written as one of those, with R, L, G and C taken from circuitRF's model at SpiceLineFreq (by default the highest frequency a source carries). It matches circuitRF's line exactly at that frequency and drifts away from it elsewhere, because constant per-unit-length values cannot follow dispersion or a skin-effect loss. The run says how far, one message per line: the largest |ΔS| between the ngspice line and circuitRF's model over the band the run resolves, and the frequency it is at. |ΔS| is an absolute difference of S-parameters; 1e-3 is negligible for most purposes, 1e-2 is visible in a reflection, and above that the ngspice result is a different line. circuitrf check reports the same number before a run. A coupled pair whose two modes lose differently is still refused, because CPL cannot represent it.

SpiceFit=yes. Writes each frequency-defined element (an SnP, a filter, an EM cell, a frequency-dependent discontinuity) as a subcircuit of the rational fit the native engine runs, and each lossy line as a lossless line plus the fit of its loss. Each carries a message saying ngspice ran circuitRF's fit of it, not the element itself. Where both apply to a line, SpiceLines=rlgc wins.

The deck. Each ngspice run leaves the deck it ran, with a map of names, in results/ngspice/<analysis>-<time>-<id>/, and its message gives the path. It is an ordinary deck, every line ending with the circuitRF part it came from: ngspice -b deck.cir runs it by hand. circuitrf netlist <bench> -o deck.cir writes it without running anything, and SpiceOptions adds an .options line of your own. ngspice's own messages appear in the Messages panel, prefixed with its name and version.

The Pulse Response example draws two benches twice, once per solver, and the two agree to the fourth digit.

Starting harmonic balance from a transient run

Harmonic balance normally starts Newton from the DC point and steps the drive up. Some circuits are far from there: a switching power amplifier whose devices only switch at full drive, a hard-driven mixer, a frequency divider whose divided solution cannot be reached by turning the drive up gradually. InitialGuess on the harmonic-balance and oscillator cards picks where Newton starts:

InitialGuess Newton starts from
dc (the default) The DC point, with the drive stepped as DriveStepping says. Every existing result is unchanged
transient The last period of a native transient run from rest at full drive, run until one period looks like the next. No drive stepping
fallback dc first; only if that does not converge, the transient start

The answer is still harmonic balance's, solved to its own Tol: the transient run only supplies the start. The run writes Seed.Periods, Seed.Settled, Seed.HbIterations and Seed.ScaledElements, and a message such as:

harmonic balance started from a transient seed: 43 periods, settled; no choke or block scaled;
harmonic balance converged in 5 Newton iterations from it.

Reach for it when a DC start does not converge or needs a long drive ladder, and when harmonic balance converges to a solution you do not believe (an undivided divider). fallback costs nothing on circuits that already converge. In a parametric sweep only the first point, and any point that fails from its neighbour's answer, is seeded.

Fast bias. A bias choke or DC block settles over its own time constant, which can be thousands of carrier periods. With SeedFastBias=yes (the default), the transient run alone uses smaller values for each inductor whose reactance at the fundamental is more than 50 times the impedance it sees, and each capacitor whose reactance is under a fiftieth of it, scaled to exactly 50 times (a fiftieth): still a choke or a block, settling in about eight periods. It does not change what harmonic balance solves: the real values are put back before Newton starts, and the answer is the same to Newton's tolerance. It shortens only the transient run. The message names each scaled part and its factor. SeedTol (default 1e-3) is how alike two periods must be, and SeedPeriods (default auto: until settled, at most 200) how long the transient run may go.

Oscillators without Fguess. With InitialGuess=transient on an oscillator analysis, the circuit is kicked (KickV, by default 1 % of the largest DC supply) at the OscProbe's node and simulated until its period and amplitude stop changing. The oscillation's own frequency, amplitude and waveforms start the solve, so Fguess is optional: without it the start-up search spans 1 kHz to 1 THz. If nothing oscillates, the run stops and quotes the start-up search's result.

Detail: Starting from a transient run and the Oscillator analysis. The Class-E with a Transient Seed example shows a switching stage seeded, beside a transient bench of the waveforms the seed came from.

From the command line

circuitrf tran bench.csch                       run every transient analysis, print the measures
circuitrf tran bench.csch --solver ngspice -o tr.npy
circuitrf netlist bench.csch -o deck.cir        the ngspice deck, or every refusal
circuitrf explain bench.csch --analysis TR1     step count, time constants, steering
circuitrf hb classe.csch                        a harmonic-balance bench with InitialGuess=transient

tran takes the same overrides as the other run verbs and runs a sweep that wraps the analysis.
